opus-5.5.text:
I think the starting point is being honest about what intelligence actually is, rather than what's easiest to measure. A lot of progress in the last few years came from language, and language is incredibly powerful, but it's also a very compressed, very human-curated slice of the world. It's what's left after someone has already done the hard work of perceiving, abstracting, and deciding what's worth saying. If you only learn from that layer, you inherit the abstractions but not necessarily the grounding underneath them.

So when I ask what world models should solve next, I usually go back to what a child or even an animal can do that our systems still struggle with. A cat can't write an essay, but it has an extremely good model of physical space: how objects move, what happens if it jumps, how to predict where something will land. That kind of intelligence is about prediction, causality, and acting in a continuous world. It's not about generating pixels that look nice. I think that's an important distinction, because right now there's a temptation to equate a world model with a really good video generator. Video generation is useful, and it's a good test, but rendering is not understanding. The real question is whether the model's internal representation supports planning, counterfactual reasoning, and adapting when something unexpected happens.

That points to a few concrete directions. One is representation: learning abstract states that capture what matters, rather than reconstructing every detail. Humans don't simulate every leaf on a tree when we predict whether a ball will clear the fence. Second is the connection between perception and action. A world model should answer "what happens if I do this?", not just "what comes next?" Third is long-horizon consistency and memory, so the model maintains a coherent world over time instead of drifting after a few seconds. And fourth, which I find underrated, is spatial intelligence: understanding 3D structure, geometry, and how you as an agent are situated in a space.

I also try to use intelligence as a guide in a slightly humbling way. Every time we think we've captured it, we find we've captured a proxy. So for me, the goal isn't to chase a benchmark, it's to keep asking: if this system were dropped into a new environment, could it figure things out the way a person would? Whatever fails that test is probably what world models should work on next.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts human language abilities with a cat’s physical and spatial intelligence, presenting intelligence in different forms across species.

r002.rationale: It says world models should return to abilities that children already have but current systems struggle with, then illustrates the kind of capability involved.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. So, when I think about intelligence as a guide, I try to start from what intelligence actually does for an agent in the world, rather than from what's easy to benchmark. And for me, the core thing is this: intelligence is the ability to build an internal representation of your environment that lets you predict, plan, and act under uncertainty. That's it. Everything else—language, reasoning, tool use—sits on top of that.

If you take that seriously, it reorders the priorities for world models quite a bit. Right now a lot of the field is measuring world models by how good the generated videos look. And I understand why—pixels are visible, they're easy to show, they're easy to get excited about. But a cat doesn't need to render a photorealistic movie of a mouse running under a table in order to know where the mouse is going to come out. It needs the right abstraction of the dynamics. So the first thing intelligence tells us is that the output of a world model should not be judged primarily on reconstruction fidelity. It should be judged on whether the representation supports the downstream things an agent needs—spatial understanding, object permanence, causal structure, counterfactual reasoning.

The second thing is about what's missing today. Language models are very intelligent in a specific sense, but they inherited a world model secondhand, through text that humans wrote about the world. That's a compressed and biased view. The parts of intelligence that are hardest for current systems are exactly the parts that humans never bothered to write down because they're too obvious: how things fall, how a scene looks from the other side of the room, what happens if I push this. So if intelligence is the guide, the next problem is grounding—learning those priors directly from visual and interactive data, in a representation that can actually be queried and reasoned over, not just sampled from.

And the third thing, which I think is underappreciated, is that intelligence is efficient. Humans learn a world model from a tiny fraction of the data we're feeding these systems, and we do it mostly through self-supervision—just watching, predicting, being surprised, updating. That tells me the learning objective matters more than scale right now. We should be asking what the right self-supervised signal is for spatial and temporal structure, in the same way that we eventually figured out the right objective for language. I don't think we've found it yet. Diffusion in pixel space is a useful tool, but I don't believe it's the final answer, because it spends enormous capacity on things that have nothing to do with intelligence.

So to summarize how I use it as a compass: ask what an agent needs to know, not what looks impressive; prioritize grounding over rendering; and look for the learning principle that gets you there with human-like data efficiency. If a research direction scores well on those three, I'm interested. If it mostly produces nicer videos, I'm happy for it, but I don't think it moves us toward intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response defines intelligence in terms of an agent’s ability to represent its environment, but does not say intelligence takes different forms across animal species.

r002.rationale: The response recommends grounding, spatial and temporal structure, and data efficiency, but does not specifically recommend tasks that young children already perform well.

astra-6.text:
I think intelligence is a useful guide if we make it concrete. What should a system be able to do after it has learned a model of the world? It should be able to predict what might happen, understand how its actions could change that outcome, and use those predictions to make decisions.

For me, that shifts the question from “Can we generate a realistic video?” to “Have we learned something that helps us act?” A video can look convincing while getting an important physical interaction wrong. And a model can be useful for planning without rendering every detail beautifully. Those capabilities are related, but we shouldn’t assume they’re the same.

So I would focus on situations where the model has to make a prediction, take an action, and then revise its understanding based on what happens. Can it handle a new situation? Can it recognize uncertainty? Can it learn from a prediction that turns out to be wrong? That gives us a more concrete way to ask whether world models are moving us toward intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response discusses intelligence through prediction, action, and learning, but does not say that intelligence takes different forms across animal species.

r002.rationale: It recommends focusing on prediction, action, and adaptation, but does not recommend tasks that young children already perform well.

sol-6.1.text:
I think intelligence is a useful guide only if we make it concrete. What does an intelligent system need to do? It needs to understand what is happening, anticipate what might happen next, and use that understanding to act. A world model should help connect those capabilities.

Predicting what comes next is a starting point, but we should ask what the model has actually learned. Can it track something when it disappears from view? Can it distinguish a change caused by its own action from a change in the environment? Can it use what it learned in a situation it hasn’t seen before?

For me, the interesting direction is to connect prediction with interaction. If a model can produce a convincing video, that demonstrates one capability. If it can help an agent choose an action, recognize that its prediction was wrong, and adapt, that gives us stronger evidence of useful understanding. So I would let those concrete capabilities guide what we build and how we evaluate it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses what intelligent systems need to do, but does not say intelligence takes different forms across animal species.

r002.rationale: It recommends concrete prediction and interaction capabilities, but does not recommend focusing on tasks that young children already perform well.
